newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition faces mounting social concerns.
newsitem.headline: German coalition faces mounting social concerns.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, increasingly split over ways to plug budget leaks to qualify for Europe's single currency, is coming under growing pressure on social issues just when it has to cut back on spending.

Public concern about the future outlook for jobs, pensions and welfare programmes is mounting while voter confidence in the ability of Kohl's party -- or any other -- to solve these problems slides, opinion pollsters and commentators say.

Strains among the coalition parties, which have now broken out into open disputes and rivalries, have further stymied the 14-year-old centre-right government and reinforced an impression of deadlock in Bonn, they added.

"Social issues are shooting up in importance like never before," said Klaus-Peter Schoeppner of the Emnid polling institute. "But instead of taking action, the politicians only think of their starting positions for the next election."

Kohl's Free Democratic (FDP) junior partners, already seen as cold neo-liberals ready to dismantle the welfare state, met with widespread cynicism when they swore at the weekend to oppose unpopular tax hikes to plug budget holes.
In a snap Forsa poll, 78 percent doubted the small party would stick to the resolution passed at its congress in Wiesbaden if Kohl chose to raise taxes this summer as expected.

At another weekend congress, the CDA trade union wing of Kohl's Christian Democrats rebelled against their moderate leaders and rejected Bonn calls for low wage agreements and the end of tax breaks for workers on evening and weekend shifts.
"Our CDA is bigger than the whole FDP -- they should listen more to us," a delegate at the Magdeburg meeting remarked.

This growing concern about the fallout from Bonn's strict austerity drive have not weakened the outlook for German participation in Europe's monetary union (EMU), which now seems more threatened by Bonn's budget problems.

Public opposition to giving up the deutschemark still runs high, but the Emnid poll showed 53 percent of Germans still trusted Kohl to represent their interests best. Only 17 percent had more faith in the SPD.
"That's not the stuff of rebellion," one CDU strategist commented to explain Kohl's continued confidence that he can sell EMU to the sceptical population.

But the poll still had several worrying messages for Kohl, whose CDU got only 36 percent, the lowest level since the last election in 1994, while the FDP scored only six percent -- too little for the tired coalition to win reelection.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) got 37 percent and its probable coalition partner, the Greens, 11 percent -- enough for an easy majority in Bonn.
Opposition support is weak, though, because the fractious SPD has yet to name a challenger to Kohl and lay out a clear alternative programme to win over uncommitted voters.
"Voters are deserting the CDU in droves, but they're going not to the SPD but rather into the pool of non-voters," Schoeppner said. "The SPD doesn't look that much better."
The Emnid poll showed 90 percent of those surveyed said that unemployment, now running at a postwar record 4.3 million, was the most pressing issue Bonn faced.

Pensions and taxes came second and third while economic policy and reducing the state debt -- two issues that normally interest prudent German voters strongly -- ranked as also-rans at under 50 percent.

"Every second German has seen close up how jobs are being slashed these days," Schoeppner commented the poll for N-TV. "So in addition to the actual level of unemployment, fear of losing a job will become a central issue in the 1998 campaign."

The SPD, which has loudly opposed government tax reform plans as a gift to the rich and questions CDU calls for cuts in some welfare state benefits, scores far better than the CDU on the issue of competence in social affairs, he added.

"Which side will win in 1998?" he asked rhetorically, "The one that demands sacrifices from all voters now to regain a competitive position in the world or the one that demands no change from most people if only the burdens on business and the rich are raised?"
